en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Saṅghādisesa Offenses
5. The Training Rule on Matchmaking At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Udāyī was a frequent visitor to families in Sāvatthī; he would approach many families.
Wherever he sees a young man without a wife or a young woman without a husband, he speaks in praise of the young woman to the parents of the young man, saying:
"The young woman of such-and-such a family is beautiful, handsome, pleasing, wise, competent, intelligent, skillful, and diligent.
That young woman is a fit match for this young man."
They spoke thus:
“Venerable sir, these people do not know us, thinking, ‘Who are these, and whose are they?
If, venerable sir, the noble one would have her given, we would bring that maiden to this young man.”
In the presence of the girl’s parents, she speaks in praise of the boy:
“The boy of such-and-such a family is handsome, beautiful, pleasing, wise, competent, intelligent, skillful, and diligent.
This girl is a fit match for that boy.”
They spoke thus:
“Venerable sir, these people do not know us— ‘Who are they, or whose are they?’—
just as one might speak to a young girl.”
“Venerable sir, if the noble one would ask for her, we would give this girl to that young man.
By this very means, he had weddings performed, marriages performed, and betrothals performed.
Now at that time, there was a certain daughter of an old courtesan who was beautiful, pleasing to behold, and graceful.
The Ājīvaka disciples from the neighboring village came and said to that courtesan,
“Noble lady, give this girl to our young man. She replied,
“Venerable sirs, I do not even know who you are or whose you are.”
"And this woman of mine has but one child, and I must go to the next village; I will not give her away.
Then those people said to the Ājīvaka disciples, "Noble sirs, for what purpose have you come?"
“Venerable sir, we asked for a certain courtesan’s daughter as a wife for our son.
She replied: ‘Venerable sirs, I do not know you— who you are or whose you are. And she is my only child;
moreover, I must go to another village. Therefore, I will not give her.”
“Why, noble sir, did you ask for that courtesan’s daughter?
Should not noble Udāyī be asked instead?
Noble Udāyī will cause her to be given.”
Then those disciples of the Ājīvakas approached the Venerable Udāyī; having approached, they said this to the Venerable Udāyī:
“Venerable sir, here we requested a certain courtesan’s daughter for our young son.
She spoke thus: ‘Noble sirs, I do not even know you—who you are or whose you are.’”
“Moreover, she has but one daughter, and I must go to another village;
I will not give her,” he said. “It would be well, venerable sir, if the noble one would cause that courtesan’s daughter to be given to our young man.
Then the Venerable Udāyī went to where that courtesan was; having approached, he spoke thus to that courtesan:
“Whose daughter will you not give?
“Sir, I do not know these people—‘Who they are’ or ‘To whom they belong.
Furthermore, she is my only daughter, and I must go to another village; I will not give her.”
“Give them to me.
I know these. “If the noble sir knows them, Venerable Sir, I shall give them.”
Then that female accountant gave her daughter to those followers of the Ājīvakas.
Having taken the girl away, those followers of the Ājīvakas lived with her for a month as a daughter-in-law;
thereafter, they lived with her as a slave.
Then that young woman sent a messenger to her mother, saying:
"I am indeed unfortunate and suffering; I find no happiness.
For only one month have they allowed me to enjoy the luxuries of a daughter-in-law."
"Then later, they will enjoy her as a slave.
Let my mother come; she shall take me away.
Then that female accountant went to those followers of the Ājīvakas; having approached them, she said this to those followers of the Ājīvakas:
“Ladies, do not enjoy this young girl as a slave;
enjoy this young girl as a daughter-in-law.
They replied thus:
“There is no exchange of food for us with you; our exchange of food is only with the ascetic.
Go away; we do not know you.”
Then that female accountant, having been dismissed by those disciples of the Ājīvakas, returned once more to Sāvatthī.
For a second time, that young woman sent a messenger to her mother, saying:
"I am indeed destitute and suffering; I find no happiness."
"For a whole month they enjoyed me with the pleasures of a daughter-in-law, but thereafter they enjoy me with the pleasures of a slave-girl.
Let my mother come; let her take me away."
Then that female accountant approached the Venerable Udāyī; having approached, she said this to the Venerable Udāyī:
"Venerable sir, it is said that this young girl is ill-fated and suffering, and finds no happiness.
For an entire month they have fed her only with the food of a daughter-in-law."
Then later, they enjoyed her as the property of a slave-girl.
You might say, venerable sirs:
"Noble ladies, do not enjoy this young girl as the property of a slave-girl."
“Enjoy this young woman as the enjoyment of a daughter-in-law.
Then the Venerable Udāyī approached those followers of the Ājīvakas; having approached them, he said to those followers of the Ājīvakas:
“Venerable sirs, do not enjoy this young woman as the enjoyment of a slave-girl.”
“Enjoy this young girl with the enjoyment due to a daughter-in-law.
They replied, “We have no business with you; our business is with courtesans.”
A recluse must be unburdened.
May you be a recluse, a true recluse; go now!
“We do not know him.
Then the Venerable Udāyī, having been disappointed by those lay followers of the Ājīvakas, returned once more to Sāvatthī.
For a third time, that young woman sent a messenger to her mother, saying:
“I am indeed unfortunate and suffering; I find no happiness.
For only one month did they maintain me with the resources of a daughter-in-law;
thereafter, they have maintained me with the resources of a slave.”
“Let my mother come; she shall take me away.
A second time, that female accountant approached the Venerable Udāyī; having approached, she said this to the Venerable Udāyī:
“Venerable sir, it is said that the young girl is in distress and suffering, and finds no ease.”
For a month they enjoyed him with the luxury of a daughter-in-law;
thereafter, they enjoyed him with the luxury of a slave-girl.
You might say, venerable sir:
“Ladies, do not enjoy this young girl as the property of a slave; enjoy this young girl as the property of a daughter-in-law.
“I was displeased by those followers of the Ājīvaka even at first;
go away!”
“I will not go.
Then that female accountant complained, grumbled, and became indignant:
“May the venerable Udāyī be so poor! May the venerable Udāyī be so miserable! May the venerable Udāyī never find happiness!”
“Venerable Udāyī, it is because of my wicked mother-in-law, my wicked father-in-law, and my wicked husband that I, a young girl, am miserable, suffering,
and finds no happiness. And so that young girl complained, grumbled, and expressed her indignation.
“May the venerable Udāyī be thus miserable; may the venerable Udāyī be thus afflicted;
may the venerable Udāyī not obtain such happiness as I do not obtain because of my wicked mother-in-law, my wicked father-in-law, and my wicked husband.”
Furthermore, there are other women who are dissatisfied with their mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, or husbands; they make such entreaties:
“May the venerable Udāyī be so destitute! May the venerable Udāyī be so miserable!
May the venerable Udāyī not find such happiness, just as we are destitute, miserable, and find no happiness because of our wicked mothers-in-law and wicked [husbands].”
“By wicked mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, and husbands.
But those women who are content with their mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, or husbands entreat him thus:
“May the venerable Udāyī be so happy; may the venerable Udāyī be so well-provided for; may the venerable Udāyī be so rich in happiness.”
“Venerable Udāyī, we are happy, well-provided for, and prospering in happiness because of our excellent mothers-in-law,
excellent fathers-in-law, and excellent husbands.
Some bhikkhus heard some women begging and others entreating.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before]... were indignant, disparaged, and complained, saying:
"How can the Venerable Udāyī engage in matchmaking?
Then those monks, having rebuked the Venerable Udāyī in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this connection, having assembled the community of monks, questioned the Venerable Udāyin:
“Is it true, Udāyin, that you have engaged in matchmaking?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, engage in matchmaking?
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so forth].
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:

“Whosoever, however, a monk should act as a go-between—conveying a man’s intent to a woman, or a woman’s intent to a man, whether for marriage or for a lover’s tryst—that is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
Thus was this training rule laid down by the Blessed One for the monks.
Now at that time, while a number of libertines were enjoying themselves in a park, they sent a messenger to a certain courtesan, saying, "Come;
we shall enjoy ourselves in the park.
She replied as follows:
“Venerable sir, I do not know who these people are or to whom they belong.
Furthermore, I have many goods and many requisites, and I must go outside the city.
Therefore, I will not go.”
Then that messenger reported this matter to those rascals.
When this was said, a certain man said this to those rascals:
“Noble sirs, why did you ask for this courtesan?”
“Surely the noble Udāyī should be told:
‘The noble Udāyī will dismiss you.
When this was said, a certain lay follower said to that man:
“Sisters, do not speak thus.
It is not permissible for the ascetics who are followers of the Sakyan to do such a thing.
Sisters, Udāyī will not do this.”
When this was said, they were amazed, wondering whether he would do it or not.
Then those scoundrels approached the Venerable Udāyī; having approached, they said to the Venerable Udāyī:
“Venerable sir, while we were enjoying ourselves here in the park, we sent a messenger to a certain courtesan named so-and-so.”
"Come, let us enjoy ourselves in the park.
She replied: "Venerable sir, I do not know you—who you are or to whom you belong;
moreover, I possess many goods and many belongings, and we must go outside the city."
“I will not go.
“It would be well, venerable sir, if the master would dismiss that courtesan.
Then the Venerable Udāyī went to where that courtesan was; having approached her, he said this to her:
“Why do you not go with them?
“Friend, I do not know who these are or whose they are.
Furthermore, I have much merchandise and many requisites, and I must travel outside the city.”
“I will not go.
“Go, friend; I know these people.
“If the noble sir knows them, Bhante, then I will go.”
Then those rakes took that courtesan and went to the park.
Thereupon, that lay follower complained, grumbled, and expressed his indignation:
"How can the venerable Udāyī engage in such momentary matchmaking?"
The bhikkhus heard that lay follower complaining, criticizing, and spreading it about.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [and so forth]... complained, criticized, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the Venerable Udāyī engage in matchmaking at that very moment?"
Then those bhikkhus, having rebuked the Venerable Udāyī in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ...“Is it true, Udāyī, that you engaged in matchmaking at that very moment?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, engage in matchmaking on that very same occasion?
This, foolish man, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so forth].
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:

“Whatever monk should act as a go-between, conveying a man’s intention to a woman, or a woman’s intention to a man, whether for the sake of marriage or for the sake of a lover, even if only for a momentary occasion, that is a *saṅghādisesa*. “Whatever monk”:
[as before].
Whoever is such a person … [as described] … “a bhikkhu” … this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”
“He should engage in matchmaking” means:
either sent by a woman, he goes into the presence of a man; or sent by a man, he goes into the presence of a woman;
or [he acts as] a go-between for a woman and a man.
She reports a man’s thought to a woman;
or she reports a woman’s thought— a woman’s thought— to a man.
"In the state of a wife" means you will become a wife; "in the state of a paramour" means...
[you will become a paramour].
You will continue to exist;
at the very least, you will exist for even a momentary flash of joy.
“An offense entailing suspension” (*saṅghādisesa*)... [as before] ...therefore it is called “an offense entailing suspension.

There are ten kinds of women: one protected by her mother, one protected by her father, one protected by both mother and father, one protected by her brother, one protected by her sister, one protected by her relatives, one protected by her clan, one protected by the Dhamma, one who has a protector, and one for whom there is legal penalty.

There are ten kinds of wives: one bought with wealth, one who lives by her own will, one who lives by her earnings, one who wears [her husband’s] clothes, one who shares the water-jar, one whose head-ornament has been taken away, a female slave who is also a wife, a female servant who is also a wife, one captured under a banner, and a momentary wife.
One protected by her mother is so called because the mother protects her, guards her, exercises authority over her, and keeps her under her control.
"Protected by her father" means that the father protects and guards her, exercises authority over her, and maintains control over her.
"Protected by both mother and father" means...
Mother and father protect, guard, exercise authority over, and bring under their control.
One "protected by a brother" means that the brother protects,
guards, exercises authority over, and brings under his control.
One protected by her sister (*bhaginirakkhitā*) is one whom a sister protects,
guards, exercises authority over, and keeps under her control.
One protected by kinsmen (*ñātirakkhitā*) is as follows:
Relatives protect, guard, exercise authority over, and bring under their control.
Those protected by clan means those of the same clan who protect,
guard, exercise authority over, and bring under their control.
Those called "protected by the Dhamma" are protected and guarded by fellow practitioners of the Dhamma; they exercise authority and maintain control over them.
Those called "with protection" [are likewise so].
She is also "taken in marriage" (pariggahitā) even while in the womb, [thinking], "This is mine. She is "encircled by a garland" (mālāguḷaparikkhittā) at the very least.
She is said to be "under penalty" (saparidaṇḍā) when a fine has been set by someone, such as: "Whoever approaches this woman named so-and-so shall pay such-and-such a fine."
One who is "purchased with wealth" (dhanakkītā) means she dwells there after having been bought with money.
One who is "dwelling by choice" (chandavāsinī) means...
A beloved person causes one who is beloved to dwell [with them].
One is said to "dwell through wealth" when one causes another to dwell by giving them wealth.
"Paṭavāsinī" means she who causes one to dwell [with him] after giving a cloth.
"Odapattakinī" means... [she who gives water from a bowl].
Having touched a water-vessel, he lets it dry.
"With the cushion removed" means having taken off the cushion, he lets it dry.
A "female slave" (dāsī) is both a female slave and a wife.
A "laborer" (kammakārī) is... [as above].
She is both a laborer and a wife.
One who is brought back as a captive after being captured under a banner is called "brought by force."
"Muhuttikā" means she is called "momentary.
A man sends a monk [with a message].
“Go, venerable sir, and say this to the woman protected by her mother named so-and-so:
‘Please become the wife of such-and-such a man, purchased for a price.
If he accepts the task, investigates, and reports back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A man sends a monk, saying:
"Go, venerable sir, speak to such-and-such a woman protected by her father...
[and so on] ...speak to such-and-such a woman protected by both her mother and father."
Speak of one protected by her brother...
speak of one protected by her sister...
speak of one protected by her kinsmen...
Speak to Gottarakkhita...
speak to Dhammarakkhita...
speak to Sārakkha...
“Speak with the threat of punishment:
‘You must indeed become the wife of such-and-such a person, purchased for money.
If she accepts, investigates, and reports back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
The Sentences for Delivering a Message:
A man sends a monk,
saying, "Go, venerable sir, and say to so-and-so, who is protected by her mother and protected by her father:..."
“‘It seems you are the wives of so-and-so, bought with wealth.
If she accepts, examines, and brings back a reply, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A man sends a message to a bhikkhu:
“Go, venerable sir, to such-and-such a woman protected by her mother and protected by her parents...
[and so on] ...a woman protected by her mother and protected by her brother...
a woman protected by her mother and protected by her sister...”
One protected by her mother and one protected by her relatives;
one protected by her mother and one protected by her clan;
one protected by her mother and one protected by the Dhamma.
“Speak to one protected by her mother and one who has a guardian,
and to one protected by her mother and subject to legal penalty, saying:
‘May you both indeed become the wives of such-and-such a man, purchased for a price.’”
If he accepts it, examines it, and brings it back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
This is the "broken wheel" [case].
A man sends a monk:
“Go, venerable sir, and say to so-and-so who is protected by her father and so-and-so who is protected by both parents:
‘May you two indeed become the wives of so-and-so, purchased for a price.
If she accepts, investigates, and reports back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A man sends a monk, saying:
"Go, venerable sir, to such-and-such a woman protected by her father and protected by her brother...
[and so on] ...to a woman protected by her father and protected by her sister..."
One protected by her father and one protected by her relatives;
one protected by her father and protected by her clan;
one protected by her father and protected by the Dhamma.
“Speak to one protected by her father and guarded,
and to one protected by her father and subject to legal penalty, saying:
‘May you indeed become the wives of such-and-such a man, purchased for a price.’”
If he accepts it, examines it, and brings it back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A man sends a message to a bhikkhu:
"Go, venerable sir, and say this to so-and-so who is protected by her father and so-and-so who is protected by her mother:..."
‘It seems you are the wives of such-and-such a person, bought with wealth.
If she accepts, examines, and brings back [the answer], there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
The root of the “bound wheel” is abbreviated.
(…) A man sent a message to a bhikkhu:
“Go, venerable sir, and say to so-and-so, who is under legal penalty and protected by her mother:
‘It seems you two are to become the wives of so-and-so for a price.’”
If he accepts it, examines it, and brings it back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A man sends a monk, saying:
"Go, venerable sir, to such-and-such a woman who is both under threat of punishment and protected by her father... [and so forth].
One who is under threat of punishment and protected by her mother and father...
one who is under threat of punishment and protected by her brother...
one who is under threat of punishment and protected by her sister...
[He commits an offense] with one who is protected by a staff and protected by kinsmen...
with one who is protected by a staff and protected by clan...
with one who is protected by a staff and protected by the Dhamma...
If she says, “Tell them with full legal authority and under protection:
‘May you indeed become the wives of such-and-such a man,
purchased for a price,’” and she accepts [the proposal], examines it, and reports back, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
The section based on a single root is finished.
In the same way, the sections based on two roots, three roots, and so on up to nine roots should be performed.
This is the section based on ten roots.
A man sends a monk, saying: "Go, venerable sir,
to such-and-such a woman who is protected by her mother, protected by her father, protected by her parents,
protected by her brother, protected by her sister, protected by her relatives, protected by her clan, and protected by the Dhamma."
"Speak thus: 'Be wives, purchased with wealth, of such-and-such a man,' specifying him as one who has protection and legal authority.
If she accepts, investigates, and reports back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
The Chapter on Dhanakkītā is finished.
A man sends a monk, saying:
"Go, venerable sir, and speak to the woman protected by her mother named so-and-so."
‘May you indeed become the wife of such-and-such a person as a Chandavāsinī … [or] a Bhogavāsinī … [or] a Paṭavāsinī …’
One who carries water in a bowl;
one whose head-covering has been removed;
a female slave and a wife.
“A wife who works for wages, one who is taken as a prize, and one who is for a limited time.”
If he accepts it, examines it, and brings it back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A man sends a message to a bhikkhu:
“Go, venerable sir, speak to so-and-so who is protected by her father …” [and so on].
Speak of one protected by her mother and father;
speak of one protected by her brother;
speak of one protected by her sister.
Speak to one protected by kinsmen...
speak to one protected by clan...
speak to one protected by the Dhamma...
“Speak with protection...
speak with a threat:
‘Indeed, become the momentary wife of such-and-such a man.’”
If he accepts it, examines it, and brings it back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
These are the sections on handing over.
A man sends a monk [with a message]:...
“Go, venerable sir, and say to so-and-so who is protected by her mother and so-and-so who is protected by her father:
‘May you both indeed become momentary wives to so-and-so.
If he accepts the mission, investigates, and returns with the report, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A man sends a monk, saying:
"Go, venerable sir, and speak to so-and-so who is protected by her mother and protected by her father... [and so on] ...to one who is protected by her mother and subject to legal penalty."
‘Are you, it seems, the momentary wives of such-and-such a person?
If she accepts [the proposal], investigates [it], and reports back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
This is the “broken wheel.”
A man sent a message to a bhikkhu:
“Go, venerable sir, and say to so-and-so who is protected by her father and so-and-so who is protected by both her parents:
‘May you two become the momentary wives of such-and-such a man.’”
If he accepts it, examines it, and brings it back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A man sends a message to a bhikkhu:
"Go, venerable sir, to such-and-such a woman protected by her father and protected by her brother... [and so forth]."
If she says, “Speak to her who is protected by her father and subject to punishment,
saying: ‘May you indeed become the momentary wives of such-and-such a man,’” and he accepts the proposal,
investigates it, and reports back, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
A man sent a monk, saying:
“Go, venerable sir, and say to so-and-so who is protected by her father and so-and-so who is protected by her mother:
‘May you both become the momentary wives of such-and-such a man.’”
If he accepts it, examines it, and brings it back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
The root of the "linked sequence" is abbreviated.
A man sends a monk: [text continues].
“Go, venerable sir, and say to such-and-such a woman who is under legal penalty and protected by her mother:
‘It seems you two should become the momentary wives of such-and-such a man.
If she accepts, investigates, and reports back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A man sends for a monk, saying:
"Go, venerable sir, speak to [a woman] who is both under threat and protected by her father...
[and so on] ...speak to one who is both under threat and guarded."
‘You are indeed the momentary wives of such-and-such a person.
If she accepts [the proposal], investigates it, and reports back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
The section based on a single root is finished.
The sections beginning with "Dumūlaka" (One Root) should be treated in exactly the same way.
This is the "Ten Root" section:
A man sends a monk—
“Go, venerable sir, and say this to [the woman] named so-and-so, who is protected by her mother, protected by her father, protected by her parents,
protected by her brother, protected by her sister, protected by her relatives, protected by her clan,
protected by the Dhamma, guarded, and subject to legal penalty:”
“‘Are you, it is said, the momentary wives of such-and-such a person?
If he accepts [the proposal], investigates, and brings back a reply, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
The cycle of “momentary wives” is finished.
A man sends a monk, saying:
"Go, venerable sir, and say to the woman protected by her mother named so-and-so:
'It seems you should become the wife, purchased with wealth, of the man named so-and-so.'"
If he accepts it, examines it, and brings it back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A man sends a message to a bhikkhu:
"Go, venerable sir, and say to such-and-such a woman protected by her mother:..."
“Be, indeed, the wife of such-and-such a man; a concubine by choice … [or] a concubine for wealth … [or] a concubine for clothing.”
One who carries water in a bowl;
one whose head-covering has been removed;
a female slave and a wife.
“A wife who works for wages, one who has been carried off under a banner,
and one who is a momentary wife.”
If he accepts it, examines it, and brings it back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
These are the sections on handing over.
A man sends a monk [with a message]:...
“Go, venerable sir, and say to the woman protected by her mother named so-and-so:
‘Become the wife of such-and-such a man, both purchased for wealth and living according to his will.
If she accepts, investigates, and reports back, there is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).
A man sends for a bhikkhu, saying:
“Go, venerable sir, and say to the woman protected by her mother named so-and-so:
‘Indeed, become the wife of such-and-such a man, purchased with wealth and living in his household’ … [as before] …”
The one bought with wealth and the one who lives in [his] clothes...
the one bought with wealth and the one from a water-jar...
the one bought with wealth and the one whose head-covering has been removed...
A wife who has been purchased with wealth and is a slave...
a wife who has been purchased with wealth and is a laborer...
a wife who has been purchased with wealth and one who was captured under a banner...
"And one bought for money, and a momentary wife.
If she accepts it, examines it, and brings it back, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.

Now at that time, a certain man commanded a certain bhikkhu, saying:
